Outline - ANOVA review - Frequentist ANOVA - Bayesian ANOVA ::: {.cell} ::: # ANOVA ## [**An**]{style="color:#b04c19"}alysis [**o**]{style="color:#5a55fa"}f [**Va**]{style="color:#dfc127"}riance (**[AN]{style="color:#b04c19"}[O]{style="color:#5a55fa"}[VA]{style="color:#dfc127"}**) [**An**]{style="color:#b04c19"}alysis [**o**]{style="color:#5a55fa"}f [**Va**]{style="color:#dfc127"}riance (**[AN]{style="color:#b04c19"}[O]{style="color:#5a55fa"}[VA]{style="color:#dfc127"}**) Method of understanding how categorical variables are related to a continuous outcome of interest Compares *between groups* to *within groups* variance to jointly compare multiple means ## ANOVA: Partitioning Variance **Total Sum of Squared Errors:** error term around the grand mean $$ SS_{total} = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 $$ If we have outcomes separated into different groups (e.g., control, treatment A, treatment B), can partition $SS_{total}$ into *between groups sums of squares* $SS_B$ and *within groups sums of squares* $SS_W$ $$ SS_{total} = SS_B + SS_W $$ [So, with $j$ indexing $J$ total groups and $i$ indexing $I$ people within a group, we can write $SS_{total}$ as...]{.fragment} ## ANOVA: Partitioning Variance **Total Sum of Squared Errors:** error term around the grand mean $$ SS_{total} = \sum_{j=1}^J \sum_{i=1}^I (x_{ij} - \bar{x})^2 $$ :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Between-Group Sum of Squares:** error between the group mean and the grand mean $$ SS_{B} = \sum_{j=1}^J n_j (\bar{x_{j}} - \bar{x})^2 $$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Within-Group Sum of Squares:** error between observations and their group mean $$ SS_{W} = \sum_{j=1}^J \sum_{i=1}^I (x_{ij} - \bar{x_{j}})^2 $$ ::: :::: ## Partitioning Variance: $SS_W$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_08_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ## ANOVA: $F$ :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Mean Square Between** $MS_B = \frac{SS_B}{J - 1} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^J n_j (\bar{x_{j}} - \bar{x})^2}{J - 1}$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Mean Square Within** $MS_W = \frac{SS_W}{N - J} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^J \sum_{i=1}^I (x_{ij} - \bar{x})^2}{N - J}$ ::: ::::
$$ F = \frac{MS_B}{MS_W} $$ ## ANOVA: Hypotheses $H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_J$ $H_1$: not $H_0$ ::: fragment Equivalent to: $H_0$: $\sigma^2_B = 0$ $H_1$: $\sigma^2_B \neq 0$ ::: ## Penguins ANOVA Example ![Dr. Kristen Gorman in the field, surrounded by penguins, at islands near Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica](https://apreshill.github.io/palmerpenguins-useR-2022/img/kristen.png){.fragment height=580} ::: footer [The untold story of palmerpenguins](https://apreshill.github.io/palmerpenguins-useR-2022/#/title-slide), photo accessed on 2026-10-16. ::: ## Penguins ANOVA Example :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Chinstrap** ![](../media/lab_08/chinstrap-penguin.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Adelie** ![](../media/lab_08/adelie-penguin.jpg) ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Gentoo** ![](../media/lab_08/gentoo-penguin.jpg) ::: :::: ::: footer [Chinstrap](https://www.secretatlas.com/assets/handbook/antarctica-destination-micro-guide/half-moon-island/full-length-photograph-of-a-chinstrap-penguin-half-moon-island-south-shetland-islands-antarctica-shutterstock-secret-atlas.jpg), [Adelie](https://res.cloudinary.com/enchanting/q_70,f_auto,w_1024,h_683,c_fit/quark-web/2024/09/SamEdmonds20-20Adelie20closeup202.jpg), and [Gentoo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c5/2020-11_Kerguelen_Islands_-_Gentoo_penguin_06_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original) penguin photos were accessed on 2026-10-15. ::: ## Penguins ANOVA Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(palmerpenguins) penguins ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181 3750 2 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186 3800 3 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18 195 3250 4 Adelie Torgersen NA NA NA NA 5 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193 3450 6 Adelie Torgersen 39.3 20.6 190 3650 7 Adelie Torgersen 38.9 17.8 181 3625 8 Adelie Torgersen 39.2 19.6 195 4675 9 Adelie Torgersen 34.1 18.1 193 3475 10 Adelie Torgersen 42 20.2 190 4250 # ℹ 334 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ## Missing Some Penguins (Data)! ::: {style="font-size:85%"} The `penguins` dataset has missing data, as do many real-life datasets. `R` represents these as `NA`s. This is something to definitively be aware of. While many functions will handle missing data in some way for you, which can be convenient, they often do so *silently* (without saying anything!). Some functions will simply return `NA`, and these often have an `na.rm` (remove `NA`s) argument. For example, :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = T) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 200.9152 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(penguins$flipper_length_mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sd(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = T) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 14.06171 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(penguins$flipper_length_mm) / length(penguins$flipper_length_mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = T) / length(penguins$flipper_length_mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 199.7471 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: ## Missing Some Penguins (Data)! Let's be proactive and remove the missing values ourselves. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_cleaned <- penguins |> filter_out(when_any(is.na(flipper_length_mm), is.na(species))) nrow(penguins); nrow(penguins_cleaned) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 344 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 342 ``` ::: ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(penguins_cleaned$flipper_length_mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 200.9152 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(penguins_cleaned$flipper_length_mm) / length(penguins_cleaned$flipper_length_mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 200.9152 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: # Frequentist ANOVA ## ANOVA: R function `aov(y ~ grouping_var, data = data)` ::: subpoint ○ `y` = outcome ::: ::: subpoint ○ `grouping_var` = name of grouping variable ::: ::: subpoint ○ `data` = dataframe that includes `grouping_var` and `y` ::: Very similar syntax to `lm(y ~ predictor, data = data)` Uses dummy coding by default `summary(model)` prints out results ## ANOVA: Example ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} flipper_model <- aov(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) summary(flipper_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) species 2 52473 26237 594.8 <2e-16 *** Residuals 339 14953 44 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: [Huge $F$-statistic!]{.fragment} [We reject the null in favor of the alternative that there is significant variation between penguin species in flipper length]{.fragment} ## Effect Sizes: Example :::: {.columns} ::: {.column .fragment width="50%"} $\eta^2$ $\frac{SS_B}{SS_T} = \frac{SS_B}{SS_B \ + \ SS_W}$ ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} effectsize::eta_squared(flipper_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Effect Size for ANOVA Parameter | Eta2 | 95% CI ------------------------------- species | 0.78 | [0.75, 1.00] - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00]. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} effectsize::eta_squared(flipper_model)$Eta2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.7782289 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="50%"} $\omega^2$ $\frac{SS_B \ - \ (J - 1)MS_w}{SS_T \ + \ MS_W}$ ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} effectsize::omega_squared(flipper_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Effect Size for ANOVA Parameter | Omega2 | 95% CI --------------------------------- species | 0.78 | [0.75, 1.00] - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00]. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} effectsize::omega_squared(flipper_model)$Omega2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.7764126 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: [In this case, $\eta^2$ and $\omega^2$ happen to be very close. Represent the proportion of variance in flipper length accounted for by differences in species.]{.fragment} ## Assumptions Visualize the distributions to check for normality, outliers, and homogeneity of variance. ::: fragment ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_08_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_cleaned |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species, color = species)) + geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, color = NA) + geom_jitter(alpha = 0.4, shape = 16, size = 3) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outliers = F) + stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = mean, size = 2.5, shape = 21) + scale_fill_manual(values = scales::col_lighter(c("#b04c19", "#5a55fa", "#dfc127"), 20)) + scale_color_manual(values = c("#b04c19", "#5a55fa", "#dfc127")) + labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper Length (mm)", caption = "Open circles represent means.") + guides(y = guide_axis(cap = "both"), x = guide_axis(cap = "both")) + coord_flip() + theme_classic(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: ::: ::: # ANOVA as a Linear Model ## ANOVA as a Linear Model Like *t*-tests, ANOVAs are just another phrasing of a linear model. Now, we have a slope term for each of our groups minus one ($J - 1$ for $J$ groups) ::: subpoint ○ Depending on the variable *coding*, the parameters present the information differently. ○ But ultimately, conducting an ANOVA explicitly as a linear model provides all the same information as conducting it in the sums of squares framework. ::: We are still interested in differences between means of groups, we just have more groups now (compared to *t*-test). Let's consider an example of an experiment where we have three groups: a control group, a treatment A group, and a treatment B group. ## ANOVA as a Linear Model ::: {style="font-size:90%"} With **dummy coding**, we use one group as a reference group and compare all others to it by using indicator variables representing belonging in each other group. $$y = \beta_0 + \beta_A \text{trt}_A + \beta_B \text{trt}_B + \epsilon$$ where $\text{trt}_A = 1$ if the participant was in treatment A and is $0$ otherwise (and similarly for $\text{trt}_B$) :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Slope Interpretations** ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 =$ mean of control group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_A =$ difference in means between control group and treatment A group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_B =$ difference in means between control group and treatment B group ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Accessing Group Means** ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 =$ mean of control group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + \beta_A =$ mean of treatment A group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + \beta_B =$ mean of treatment B group ::: ::: :::: ::: ## ANOVA as a Linear Model ::: {style="font-size:90%"} With **dummy coding**, we use one group as a reference group and compare all others to it by using indicator variables representing belonging in each other group. $$y = \beta_0 + \beta_A \text{trt}_A + \beta_B \text{trt}_B + \epsilon$$ where $\text{trt}_A = 1$ if the participant was in treatment A and is $0$ otherwise (and similarly for $\text{trt}_B$) ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2" layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_08_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_08_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-2.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## ANOVA as a Linear Model ::: {style="font-size:90%"} With **effect coding**, we let the grand mean be the "reference" point and examine $J - 1$ groups as by their deviation from the grand mean. $$y = \beta_0 + \beta_A x_A + \beta_B x_B + \epsilon$$ where $x_A = 1$ if the participant was in treatment A, $x_A = -1$ if the participant was in the control, and is $0$ otherwise. Similarly, $x_B = 1$ if the participant was in treatment B, $x_B = -1$ if the participant was in the control, and is $0$ otherwise. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Slope Interpretations** ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 =$ overall grand mean ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_A =$ deviation of treatment A from grand mean ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_B =$ deviation of treatment B from grand mean ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Accessing Group Means** ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 =$ overall grand mean ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + \beta_A =$ mean of treatment A group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + \beta_B =$ mean of treatment B group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + (-1)\beta_A + (-1)\beta_B =$ mean of control group ::: ::: :::: ::: ## ANOVA as a Linear Model ::: {style="font-size:90%"} With **effect coding**, we let the grand mean be the "reference" point and examine $J - 2$ groups by their deviation from the grand mean. $$y = \beta_0 + \beta_A x_A + \beta_B x_B + \epsilon$$ where $x_A = 1$ if the participant was in treatment A, $x_A = -1$ if the participant was in the control, and is $0$ otherwise. Similarly, $x_B = 1$ if the participant was in treatment B, $x_B = -1$ if the participant was in the control, and is $0$ otherwise. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2" layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_08_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_08_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-2.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## ANOVA as a Linear Model in R We can conduct ANOVAs explicitly as linear models with `lm(outcome ~ grouping_variable, data = data)`. :::: {.columns .fragment} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} flipper_model_lm <- lm(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) summary(flipper_model_lm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -17.9536 -4.8235 0.0464 4.8130 20.0464 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 189.9536 0.5405 351.454 < 2e-16 *** speciesChinstrap 5.8699 0.9699 6.052 3.79e-09 *** speciesGentoo 27.2333 0.8067 33.760 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 6.642 on 339 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.7782, Adjusted R-squared: 0.7769 F-statistic: 594.8 on 2 and 339 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column style="font-size:80%" width="50%"} With dummy coding, ::: subpoint ○ `(Intercept)` = mean of reference group (here, $\mu_\text{Adelie}$) ::: ::: subpoint ○ `speciesChinstrap` = difference between target group and reference group (here, $\mu_\text{Chinstrap} - \mu_\text{Adelie}$) ::: ::: subpoint ○ `speciesGentoo` = difference between target group and reference group (here, $\mu_\text{Gentoo} - \mu_\text{Adelie}$) ::: ::: :::: ## Changing to Effect Coding We can tell `R` we want to use effect coding instead of dummy coding; we don't have to manually create the effect coding columns ourselves. We need to set the `contrasts` setting of our grouping variable to `contr.sum`. Everything you run after that will use effect coding. ::: fragment :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Before (default)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrasts(penguins_cleaned$species) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chinstrap Gentoo Adelie 0 0 Chinstrap 1 0 Gentoo 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **After** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrasts(penguins_cleaned$species) <- contr.sum contrasts(penguins_cleaned$species) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] Adelie 1 0 Chinstrap 0 1 Gentoo -1 -1 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} flipper_model_lm_effect <- lm(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) ``` ::: ::: [What two effects will we see in the slope parameters?]{.fragment} [Adelie and Chinstrap!]{.fragment} ## Changing to Effect Coding We can tell `R` we want to use effect coding instead of dummy coding; we don't have to manually create the effect coding columns ourselves. We need to set the `contrasts` setting of our grouping variable to `contr.sum`. Everything you run after that will use effect coding. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(flipper_model_lm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins_cleaned) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -17.9536 -4.8235 0.0464 4.8130 20.0464 Coefficients: Estimate Std. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
